title: GST (Inter P3B)
description: GST for CA Intermediate Paper 3 Section B (ICAI new scheme, attempts from May 2027): supply, levy, place of supply, exemptions, time and value, ITC, registration, invoicing, e-way bill, payment and returns. Based on the CGST and IGST Acts as amended by the Finance Act 2026, with the GST 2.0 rate structure in force from 22 September 2025.

chapters.title: GST in India: Introduction and Constitutional Framework
chapters.summary: Why GST replaced the old indirect taxes, how the 101st Constitution Amendment gives the Centre and States concurrent power, and how CGST, SGST, UTGST and IGST fit together.
chapters.lawAsOf: Constitution (101st Amendment) Act 2016; CGST, IGST and UTGST Acts 2017 as amended by the Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: From a cascading regime to a dual GST
lesson.body:
Before 1 July 2017 the Centre levied central excise, service tax, CVD and SAD, while States levied VAT, entry tax, entertainment tax, luxury tax and purchase tax. The Centre could not tax sales and the States could not tax services, so each tax was charged on a base that already included the other tax. Credit of one tax could not be set off against the other. This is **cascading** (tax on tax).

GST is a destination-based, multi-stage tax on the **supply** of goods or services or both, with seamless input tax credit (ITC) at each stage. Only the value added at each stage bears tax in effect, and the final burden falls on the consumer.

India follows a **dual GST**: the Centre and the State tax the same transaction at the same time.

| Type of supply | Taxes levied | Law |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Intra-State (within one State) | CGST + SGST | CGST Act + respective SGST Act |
| Intra-UT (UT without legislature) | CGST + UTGST | CGST Act + UTGST Act |
| Inter-State, imports, supplies to or by SEZ | IGST | IGST Act |

UTGST applies in Union Territories without a legislature: Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Ladakh and Chandigarh. Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir have legislatures, so they levy SGST.

lesson.heading: Constitutional framework
lesson.body:
The **Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016** made GST possible.

| Article | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| 246A(1) | Parliament and State legislatures both have power to make laws on GST (concurrent power) |
| 246A(2) | Parliament has exclusive power over GST on inter-State supplies |
| 269A | GST on inter-State supplies (IGST) is levied and collected by the Government of India and apportioned between the Union and States as per GST Council recommendations; imports are deemed inter-State |
| 279A | Constitutes the GST Council |
| 366(12A) | Defines GST: any tax on supply of goods or services or both, except tax on supply of alcoholic liquor for human consumption |
| 366(26A) | Services: anything other than goods |

**GST Council (Article 279A):** chaired by the Union Finance Minister; members are the Union Minister of State for Revenue or Finance and the Finance (or other nominated) Minister of each State. Quorum is one-half of total members. Decisions need at least three-fourths of the weighted votes of members present and voting: the Centre's vote carries one-third weight and all States together carry two-thirds.

Petroleum crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit (petrol), natural gas and aviation turbine fuel are within the GST definition, but GST on them applies only from a date the Council recommends (section 9(2) CGST Act). Until then, central excise and State VAT continue on them. Alcoholic liquor for human consumption is outside GST altogether.

lesson.heading: Taxes subsumed and taxes outside GST
lesson.body:
| Subsumed in GST | Not subsumed (continue) |
| --- | --- |
| Central excise (except on specified tobacco and petroleum products), service tax, CVD, SAD | Basic customs duty |
| State VAT / sales tax (except on the five petroleum products and alcoholic liquor) | Stamp duty, property tax |
| Entry tax, octroi, purchase tax, luxury tax | Electricity duty |
| Entertainment tax (other than that levied by local bodies) | State excise on alcoholic liquor |
| Taxes on lottery, betting and gambling | Central excise on petroleum products and tobacco |

**GST 2.0 (from 22 September 2025):** the 56th GST Council meeting replaced the four main slabs (5%, 12%, 18%, 28%) with two main slabs of **5%** and **18%** plus a special **40%** rate for sin and luxury goods. Nil, 0.25% and 3% rates continue for specified goods. Compensation cess has been wound down: from 1 February 2026 tobacco products and pan masala moved to 40% GST, with additional central excise duty on tobacco and a separate Health and National Security Cess on pan masala outside GST.

The CGST Act caps the CGST rate at 20% and the IGST Act caps the IGST rate at 40%.

lesson.heading: Worked example and common mistakes
lesson.body:
A dealer in Pune sells goods worth ₹4,00,000 at 18%: (a) to a buyer in Nagpur, (b) to a buyer in Indore, (c) to a buyer in Chandigarh.

| Supply | Nature | Tax |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pune to Nagpur | Intra-State (Maharashtra) | CGST 36,000 + SGST 36,000 |
| Pune to Indore | Inter-State | IGST 72,000 |
| Pune to Chandigarh | Inter-State (State to UT) | IGST 72,000 |

**Common mistakes:**
- Charging UTGST on a supply from a State to a UT. UTGST applies only to supplies within a UT; State-to-UT is inter-State and attracts IGST.
- Saying petrol is outside the Constitution's GST definition. It is inside the definition; only the levy date is deferred.
- Saying alcohol for industrial use is outside GST. Only alcoholic liquor for **human consumption** is excluded.
- Treating the GST Council as a body that makes law. It recommends; Parliament and State legislatures legislate and governments notify.

keyPoints: 101st Constitution Amendment Act 2016: Articles 246A (concurrent power), 269A (IGST), 279A (GST Council), 366(12A) (GST definition).
Intra-State: CGST + SGST/UTGST. Inter-State, imports and SEZ supplies: IGST.
GST Council decision: 3/4 of weighted votes of members present and voting; Centre 1/3 weight, States 2/3; quorum 50% of members.
Alcoholic liquor for human consumption is outside GST; five petroleum products are within GST but levy is deferred until the Council recommends a date (section 9(2)).
GST 2.0 from 22 September 2025: main slabs 5% and 18%, special rate 40%; nil, 0.25% and 3% for specified goods.
Maximum rates under the Acts: CGST 20%, IGST 40%.
UTGST only for UTs without legislature; Delhi, Puducherry and J&K levy SGST.

cases.title: Case: Konkan Agro Foods
cases.body:
Konkan Agro Foods is registered in Pune, Maharashtra. During October 2026 it records the following (all values exclusive of GST):

| No. | Transaction | Value (₹) | Rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Sale of packaged food to a dealer in Mumbai | 5,00,000 | 5% |
| 2 | Sale of packaged food to a dealer in Panaji, Goa | 3,00,000 | 5% |
| 3 | Sale of kitchen equipment to a hotel in Chandigarh | 2,00,000 | 18% |
| 4 | Purchase of high speed diesel for its generator | 1,00,000 | - |

The accountant wants to know which taxes apply to each item.

questions.prompt: Which Article of the Constitution gives both Parliament and State legislatures the power to make laws on GST?
options: Article 246A
Article 269A
Article 279A
Article 366(12A)
questions.explanation: Article 246A(1) confers concurrent power to make laws on GST. Article 246A(2) reserves inter-State supplies to Parliament. Article 269A deals with IGST, 279A with the GST Council and 366(12A) defines GST.

questions.prompt: A decision of the GST Council is taken by:
options: Simple majority of members present
Not less than three-fourths of the weighted votes of members present and voting
Two-thirds of all members of the Council
Unanimous vote of all State Finance Ministers
questions.explanation: Article 279A(9): three-fourths of the weighted votes of members present and voting. The Centre's vote has one-third weight and all States together two-thirds, so neither side can pass a proposal alone.

questions.prompt: A supply from a registered supplier in Mohali (Punjab) to a recipient in Chandigarh attracts:
options: CGST + SGST
CGST + UTGST
IGST
UTGST only
questions.explanation: Location of supplier (Punjab) and place of supply (Chandigarh, a UT) are in different States/UTs, so it is inter-State and IGST applies. UTGST is charged only on supplies within a UT.

questions.prompt: Under the GST 2.0 rate structure effective from 22 September 2025, which set describes the two main slabs and the special rate?
questions.explanation: The 56th GST Council meeting approved a two-slab structure of 5% and 18%, with a special 40% rate for sin and luxury goods. The 12% and 28% slabs were largely removed. Nil, 0.25% and 3% rates continue for specified goods.

questions.prompt: High speed diesel and petrol are outside the definition of GST in the Constitution.
questions.explanation: They are inside the definition. Only alcoholic liquor for human consumption is excluded by Article 366(12A). GST on the five petroleum products applies from a date to be notified on the GST Council's recommendation (section 9(2) CGST Act); until then central excise and State VAT continue.

questions.prompt: Which of the following taxes were subsumed in GST? Select all that apply.
options: Service tax
Basic customs duty
State VAT on consumer goods
Entry tax
Stamp duty
questions.explanation: Service tax, VAT on goods other than petroleum products and alcoholic liquor, and entry tax were subsumed. Basic customs duty and stamp duty continue outside GST.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: GST on supplies in the course of inter-State trade or commerce is levied and collected by the Government of India under Article ___ of the Constitution.
questions.explanation: Article 269A provides that IGST is levied and collected by the Union and apportioned between the Union and the States on the GST Council's recommendation. Imports are deemed inter-State supplies for this purpose.

questions.prompt: A registered supplier in Jaipur sells goods to a buyer in Udaipur for ₹2,40,000 (exclusive of GST). The rate is 18%. Compute the CGST payable on this supply. Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation:
Jaipur and Udaipur are both in Rajasthan, so the supply is intra-State: CGST 9% + SGST 9%.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Value | 2,40,000 |
| CGST @ 9% | 21,600 |
| SGST @ 9% | 21,600 |
| Total GST | 43,200 |

questions.prompt: A Kolkata supplier sells goods to a Bhubaneswar buyer for a total of ₹2,36,000, inclusive of GST at 18%. Compute the IGST included in this amount. Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation:
West Bengal to Odisha is inter-State, so IGST applies.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Inclusive price | 2,36,000 |
| Value = 2,36,000 x 100/118 | 2,00,000 |
| IGST = 2,36,000 x 18/118 | 36,000 |

questions.prompt: Which tax applies to transaction 3?
options: IGST
CGST + UTGST
CGST + SGST of Maharashtra
UTGST only
questions.explanation: The supplier is in Maharashtra and the place of supply is Chandigarh. Different State/UT means inter-State supply, so IGST at 18% (₹36,000) applies.

questions.prompt: Compute the total GST (CGST + SGST + IGST) payable by Konkan Agro Foods on its outward supplies (transactions 1 to 3). Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation:
| Transaction | Nature | Tax (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Mumbai, 5,00,000 @ 5% | Intra-State | CGST 12,500 + SGST 12,500 = 25,000 |
| 2. Goa, 3,00,000 @ 5% | Inter-State | IGST 15,000 |
| 3. Chandigarh, 2,00,000 @ 18% | Inter-State | IGST 36,000 |
| **Total** | | **76,000** |

Transaction 4 is a purchase, not an outward supply.

questions.prompt: What is the correct tax position of transaction 4 (high speed diesel)?
options: GST at 18% with full ITC
Central excise duty and State VAT apply, as GST on diesel has not yet been notified to apply
Diesel is permanently outside GST under the Constitution
Only IGST applies because diesel is a petroleum product
questions.explanation: High speed diesel is within the constitutional definition of GST, but section 9(2) CGST Act defers the levy until a date notified on the Council's recommendation. Until then central excise and State VAT apply, and no GST credit arises.

questions.prompt: Explain the features of the dual GST model adopted in India and the constitutional provisions that enable it.
questions.answer:
- India follows a concurrent dual GST: the Centre and States levy GST on the same supply at the same time.
- Article 246A gives Parliament and State legislatures concurrent power over GST; Article 246A(2) gives Parliament exclusive power over inter-State supplies.
- Intra-State supplies attract CGST (CGST Act) and SGST (State GST Acts) or UTGST in UTs without legislature.
- Inter-State supplies and imports attract IGST, levied and collected by the Centre under Article 269A and apportioned between the Centre and the destination State.
- Article 279A constitutes the GST Council to recommend rates, exemptions, thresholds and model laws.
- GST is destination based: tax revenue goes to the State where the supply is consumed.
- Seamless ITC removes cascading; cross-utilisation of CGST and SGST credit is not allowed, but IGST credit can be used against all three.

questions.prompt: Describe the composition and voting mechanism of the GST Council and list four matters on which it makes recommendations.
questions.answer:
- Composition (Article 279A(2)): Union Finance Minister (Chairperson), Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance, and the Minister in charge of Finance or Taxation (or any other nominated minister) of each State.
- Quorum: one-half of the total number of members.
- Voting: every decision needs at least three-fourths of the weighted votes of members present and voting. The Central Government's vote has one-third weight and the votes of all State Governments together have two-thirds weight.
- Recommendations (Article 279A(4)) include: taxes to be subsumed; goods and services to be taxed or exempted; model GST laws and principles of place of supply; threshold limits; rates including floor rates with bands; special rates for a specified period to raise resources during a disaster; special provisions for special category States.
- Article 279A(5): the Council recommends the date from which GST is levied on the five petroleum products.

chapters.title: Supply under GST
chapters.summary: The taxable event under GST: the scope of supply in section 7, Schedules I, II and III, and the treatment of composite and mixed supplies under section 8.
chapters.lawAsOf: CGST Act 2017 (sections 7, 8 and Schedules I to III) as amended by the Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Scope of supply: section 7
lesson.body:
Supply is the taxable event under GST. Section 7(1) says supply includes:

| Clause | Coverage |
| --- | --- |
| 7(1)(a) | All forms of supply of goods or services or both, such as sale, transfer, barter, exchange, licence, rental, lease or disposal, made or agreed to be made **for a consideration** by a person **in the course or furtherance of business** |
| 7(1)(aa) | Activities or transactions by a person, other than an individual, for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration, to its members or constituents (and vice versa). The person and its members are deemed two separate persons (inserted by Finance Act 2021, effective from 1 July 2017) |
| 7(1)(b) | Import of services for a consideration, **whether or not** in the course or furtherance of business |
| 7(1)(c) | Activities in **Schedule I**, made or agreed to be made **without consideration** |

Section 7(1A): once an activity is a supply, Schedule II decides whether it is a supply of goods or of services. Section 7(2): activities in **Schedule III**, and specified activities of the Government or local authorities as public authorities, are neither supply of goods nor supply of services.

Business (section 2(17)) is wide: any trade, commerce, manufacture, profession or vocation, whether or not for profit, and anything incidental or ancillary to it, including supply or acquisition of capital goods and services in connection with commencement or closure of business.

lesson.heading: Schedules I, II and III
lesson.body:
**Schedule I: supply even without consideration**
- Permanent transfer or disposal of business assets on which ITC has been availed.
- Supply between related persons or distinct persons (section 25) in the course or furtherance of business. Gifts by an employer to an employee up to ₹50,000 in value in a financial year are not treated as supply.
- Supply of goods by a principal to an agent who undertakes to supply them on behalf of the principal, and by an agent to a principal who receives them on the principal's behalf.
- Import of services by a person from a related person or from any of its establishments outside India, in the course or furtherance of business.

**Schedule II: goods or services?** Examples: transfer of title in goods is a supply of goods; transfer of right in goods without transfer of title is a supply of services; lease or renting of land or building is a supply of services; works contract is a supply of services; supply of food or drink as part of a service (restaurant) is a supply of services.

**Schedule III: neither goods nor services**
- Services by an employee to the employer in the course of employment.
- Services by any court or tribunal; functions of MPs, MLAs and members of local authorities; duties of constitutional office holders.
- Services of funeral, burial, crematorium or mortuary.
- Sale of land and, subject to para 5 of Schedule II, sale of a completed building.
- Actionable claims, other than specified actionable claims (betting, casinos, gambling, horse racing, lottery and online money gaming).
- Supply of goods from a place outside India to another place outside India without entering India (merchant trade), high-sea sales before clearance for home consumption, and supply of warehoused goods before clearance for home consumption.

lesson.heading: Composite and mixed supply: section 8
lesson.body:
| Point | Composite supply (section 2(30)) | Mixed supply (section 2(74)) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nature | Two or more supplies **naturally bundled** in the ordinary course of business | Two or more individual supplies made together for a **single price**, not naturally bundled |
| Principal supply | One supply is predominant (principal supply, section 2(90)) | No principal supply |
| Tax treatment | Rate of the **principal supply** | Rate of the item with the **highest rate** |
| Example | Goods packed, insured and transported by the supplier; a laptop sold with charger and bag | A Diwali hamper of sweets, dry fruits and an electric lamp for one price |

Test for natural bundling: do customers normally expect the items together, are they advertised as a package, does one element have no use without the other? A works contract and restaurant service are specifically deemed composite supplies of services by Schedule II.

lesson.heading: Worked example and common mistakes
lesson.body:
A trader sells 100 gift packs at ₹5,000 each. Each pack holds dry fruits (taxable at 5%) and a decorative lamp (taxable at 18%). The items are not naturally bundled, so this is a mixed supply taxed at the highest rate.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Value 100 x 5,000 | 5,00,000 |
| GST @ 18% (highest rate) | 90,000 |

**Common mistakes:**
- Treating every free transfer as non-taxable. Branch transfers to a separately registered branch (distinct person) are supplies under Schedule I.
- Applying the ₹50,000 gift limit to gifts to customers. The limit is only for employer-to-employee gifts.
- Saying sale of land attracts GST. Sale of land is in Schedule III.
- Forgetting that import of services for consideration is a supply even when not for business.

keyPoints: Section 7(1)(a): supply for consideration in the course or furtherance of business; 7(1)(b): import of services for consideration even if not for business.
Section 7(1)(aa): club or association to its members is a supply (retrospective from 1 July 2017).
Schedule I: supply without consideration - business assets with ITC, related or distinct persons, principal-agent, import of services from related person.
Employer gifts to an employee up to ₹50,000 per financial year are not a supply.
Schedule III: employee services, court services, funeral services, sale of land and completed building, most actionable claims, merchant trade, high-sea sales, warehoused goods before home clearance.
Composite supply: rate of principal supply. Mixed supply: highest rate.

cases.title: Case: Vardhaman Electricals
cases.body:
Vardhaman Electricals is a registered dealer in Jaipur. Its transactions in November 2026 are:

| No. | Transaction | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Sale of air coolers to retail customers | 2,00,000 |
| 2 | Stock of coolers sent free of cost to its own branch in Ahmedabad, separately registered in Gujarat (open market value) | 1,00,000 |
| 3 | Coolers sent to an agent in Kota who will sell them in his own name on behalf of Vardhaman (open market value) | 80,000 |
| 4 | Sale of old office furniture | 30,000 |
| 5 | Sale of a plot of land held as a business asset | 40,00,000 |

All amounts are exclusive of GST.

questions.prompt: Mr Rohan, a salaried individual, pays a US-based consultant for advice on his personal investments. Is this a supply under GST?
options: No, because it is not in the course or furtherance of business
Yes, because import of services for consideration is a supply whether or not in the course of business
Yes, but only if Rohan is registered under GST
No, because services from outside India are covered by customs law
questions.explanation: Section 7(1)(b) covers import of services for a consideration whether or not in the course or furtherance of business. Whether any exemption applies is a separate question; the activity is still a supply.

questions.prompt: An employer gifts a smartphone worth ₹45,000 to an employee in a financial year; no other gifts are given to that employee. The GST position is:
options: Supply under Schedule I, taxable on open market value
Not a supply, because gifts up to ₹50,000 per employee per financial year are excluded
Supply under section 7(1)(a)
Exempt supply
questions.explanation: Employer and employee are related persons, but the proviso to para 2 of Schedule I excludes gifts up to ₹50,000 in value in a financial year by an employer to an employee.

questions.prompt: A television sold with a wall-mount kit and free installation for one price is best classified as:
options: Mixed supply taxed at the highest rate
Composite supply taxed at the rate of the television
Two separate supplies
Not a supply
questions.explanation: The kit and installation are naturally bundled with the TV, and the TV is the principal supply. Under section 8(a) the whole composite supply is taxed at the rate applicable to the TV.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a supply of services under Schedule II?
options: Transfer of title in goods
Renting of a commercial building
Sale of a completed building after issue of completion certificate
Sale of land
questions.explanation: Para 2(b) of Schedule II treats any lease or letting out of a building for business or commerce as a supply of services. Transfer of title in goods is a supply of goods. Sale of land and of a completed building are Schedule III items.

questions.prompt: Under section 7(1)(aa), supply of food by a cooperative club to its members for a charge is a supply, because the club and its members are deemed separate persons.
questions.explanation: Section 7(1)(aa), inserted by the Finance Act 2021 with effect from 1 July 2017, covers activities of a person other than an individual to its members or constituents for consideration, and deems them two separate persons. This overrides the mutuality argument.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are neither supply of goods nor supply of services under Schedule III? Select all that apply.
options: Services by an employee to the employer in the course of employment
Sale of a plot of land
Lottery tickets sold by an authorised distributor
High-sea sale of imported goods before clearance for home consumption
Renting of a residential flat
questions.explanation: Employee services, sale of land and high-sea sales are in Schedule III. Lottery is a specified actionable claim and is taxable. Renting of a flat is a supply of services (it may or may not be exempt).

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: activities specified in Schedule ___ of the CGST Act are treated neither as a supply of goods nor a supply of services.
questions.explanation: Section 7(2)(a) read with Schedule III lists activities that are neither supply of goods nor services, such as employee services, sale of land and funeral services.

questions.prompt: A shop sells 200 festive hampers at ₹2,500 each. Each hamper contains sweets (5%), dry fruits (5%) and a steel serving tray (18%). The items are not naturally bundled. Compute the GST payable. Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation:
The hamper is a mixed supply under section 2(74): items sold together for a single price, not naturally bundled. Section 8(b) applies the highest rate.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Value 200 x 2,500 | 5,00,000 |
| GST @ 18% | 90,000 |

questions.prompt: A dealer sells a laptop with a charger, a carry bag and a one-year standard warranty for a single price of ₹63,000 (exclusive of GST). Assume laptops are taxable at 18% and carry bags at 5%. Compute the GST payable. Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation:
The accessories and standard warranty are naturally bundled with the laptop, which is the principal supply. This is a composite supply taxed at the rate of the laptop.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Value | 63,000 |
| GST @ 18% | 11,340 |

questions.prompt: What is the GST status of transaction 2 (free stock sent to the Ahmedabad branch)?
options: Not a supply because there is no consideration
Supply under Schedule I because the branches are distinct persons
Exempt as a stock transfer
Supply only if the branch later sells the goods
questions.explanation: Establishments of the same person registered in different States are distinct persons (section 25(4)). Para 2 of Schedule I treats supply between distinct persons in the course of business as a supply even without consideration. It is an inter-State supply attracting IGST.

questions.prompt: Compute the total value of taxable supplies of Vardhaman Electricals for November 2026. Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation:
| No. | Treatment | Value (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Supply for consideration, section 7(1)(a) | 2,00,000 |
| 2 | Distinct persons, Schedule I | 1,00,000 |
| 3 | Principal to agent, Schedule I | 80,000 |
| 4 | Sale of business asset for consideration, section 7(1)(a) | 30,000 |
| 5 | Sale of land, Schedule III | Nil |
| **Total** | | **4,10,000** |

The ITC condition in para 1 of Schedule I matters only for disposals without consideration; furniture sold for a price is a supply under section 7(1)(a).

questions.prompt: How is transaction 5 (sale of land) treated?
options: Supply of goods at 18%
Supply of services at 18%
Neither a supply of goods nor services
Exempt supply of goods
questions.explanation: Para 5 of Schedule III: sale of land is neither a supply of goods nor a supply of services. No GST is payable.

questions.prompt: Examine whether each of the following is a supply under the CGST Act. Give reasons.
questions.data:
- (a) A doctor sells his personal car, used only by his family and bought without ITC, to a friend for ₹3,00,000.
- (b) A company permanently transfers an office printer (ITC availed) free of cost to a charitable trust.
- (c) A Delhi company receives management services free of cost from its holding company in Singapore.
- (d) A director of a company receives salary as a whole-time director, with TDS deducted under the salary provisions.
- (e) A car dealer exchanges a new car for an old car plus cash.
questions.answer:
| Item | Supply? | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| (a) | No | There is consideration, but the car is a personal asset and the sale is not in the course or furtherance of his profession, so section 7(1)(a) is not attracted. |
| (b) | Yes | Para 1 of Schedule I: permanent disposal of business assets on which ITC was availed, even without consideration. |
| (c) | Yes | Para 4 of Schedule I: import of services from a related person outside India in the course of business, even without consideration. |
| (d) | No | Para 1 of Schedule III: services by an employee to employer. A whole-time director whose remuneration is treated as salary is an employee. |
| (e) | Yes | Barter and exchange are forms of supply under section 7(1)(a); the old car is part of the consideration. |

questions.prompt: Distinguish between composite supply and mixed supply, with their tax treatment and one example each.
questions.answer:
- Composite supply (section 2(30)): two or more taxable supplies naturally bundled and supplied together in the ordinary course of business, one of which is the principal supply. Taxed at the rate of the principal supply (section 8(a)). Example: goods sold with packing, transport and insurance arranged by the supplier.
- Mixed supply (section 2(74)): two or more individual supplies made together for a single price where the supply is not a composite supply. Taxed at the highest rate applicable to any item (section 8(b)). Example: a pack of chocolates, a cake and a toy sold for one price.
- Test: whether the elements are normally provided together, advertised as a package and whether one element is the main reason for buying.
- If items are priced separately, each is a separate supply taxed at its own rate.

lesson.heading: The levy: section 9 CGST and section 5 IGST
lesson.body:
Section 9(1) CGST levies CGST on all **intra-State** supplies of goods or services or both, except alcoholic liquor for human consumption, on the value determined under section 15, at rates notified on the Council's recommendation, not exceeding 20%. Section 5(1) IGST does the same for **inter-State** supplies, with a ceiling of 40%. IGST on imported goods is levied with customs duty under the Customs Tariff Act.

| Sub-section | Who pays |
| --- | --- |
| 9(1) | Supplier (forward charge) |
| 9(2) | Five petroleum products taxed from a date to be notified |
| 9(3) | Recipient, for notified categories of goods or services (reverse charge) |
| 9(4) | Notified class of registered recipients, on notified supplies from unregistered suppliers |
| 9(5) | Electronic commerce operator (ECO), for notified services supplied through it |

Under 9(5) the ECO is deemed the supplier for: passenger transport by radio taxi, motor cab, maxi cab and motor cycle; accommodation in hotels, inns, guest houses and similar places (unless the supplier is liable to register under section 22(1)); housekeeping services such as plumbing and carpentry (unless the supplier is liable to register); and restaurant services (other than at specified premises).

lesson.heading: Reverse charge: key notified services and goods
lesson.body:
| Service under section 9(3) | Supplier | Recipient who pays |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Legal services | Individual advocate or firm of advocates | Business entity in taxable territory |
| Arbitral tribunal services | Arbitral tribunal | Business entity |
| Sponsorship services | Any person | Body corporate or partnership firm |
| Services as director | Director of a company or body corporate (other than as employee) | The company or body corporate |
| Insurance agent services | Insurance agent | Insurer |
| Recovery agent services | Recovery agent | Bank, financial institution, NBFC |
| Transfer of copyright in a literary work by an author | Author (unless opted to pay forward charge) | Publisher, music company, producer |
| Security services (supply of security personnel) | Any person other than a body corporate | Registered person (with specified exclusions) |
| Renting of residential dwelling | Any person | Registered person |
| Services by Government (with exclusions) | Central/State Government, local authority | Business entity |

Goods under RCM include cashew nuts (not shelled or peeled), bidi wrapper leaves, tobacco leaves and raw cotton supplied by an agriculturist, and used vehicles or seized goods sold by the Government.

Recipient's points under RCM:
- Must register (section 24) irrespective of turnover.
- Must pay RCM tax through the **electronic cash ledger** (section 49(4) read with the Explanation to section 49); ITC cannot be used.
- Can take ITC of RCM tax paid if the input or input service is used for business and not blocked.
- Must issue a self-invoice where the supplier is unregistered, and a payment voucher.

lesson.heading: Composition levy: section 10
lesson.body:
| Point | Section 10(1) scheme | Section 10(2A) scheme |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who | Manufacturers, traders, restaurants (not serving alcohol) | Suppliers of services or mixed suppliers not eligible for 10(1) |
| Turnover limit (aggregate turnover of preceding FY) | ₹1.5 crore (₹75 lakh in specified special category States) | ₹50 lakh |
| Rate (CGST + SGST) | Manufacturer 1% of turnover in State; trader 1% of turnover of taxable supplies in State; restaurant 5% of turnover in State | 6% of turnover in State |
| Services allowed | Up to higher of 10% of turnover in State in preceding FY or ₹5 lakh | Main activity is services |

**Not eligible** for section 10(1): suppliers of services (other than restaurant service), suppliers of non-taxable goods, persons making inter-State outward supplies, persons supplying goods through an ECO required to collect TCS, casual and non-resident taxable persons, and manufacturers of notified goods such as ice cream, pan masala and tobacco products.

**Conditions:** no ITC; cannot collect tax from customers; issue a **bill of supply** with the words 'composition taxable person, not eligible to collect tax on supplies'; display 'composition taxable person' at the place of business; pay tax quarterly in CMP-08 and file annual return GSTR-4. RCM liability is paid at normal rates. The option applies to all registrations under the same PAN. Once aggregate turnover in the current year crosses the limit, the option lapses from that day.

lesson.heading: Rate structure after GST 2.0
lesson.body:
From 22 September 2025 the rate notifications were rewritten on the 56th GST Council's recommendations:

| Slab | Typical coverage |
| --- | --- |
| Nil / exempt | Fresh produce, unbranded staples, specified essentials; individual life and health insurance services exempt from 22 September 2025 |
| 0.25% / 3% | Rough diamonds / gold, silver, jewellery |
| 5% | Common-use goods and essentials; restaurant services (other than specified premises) without ITC; hotel accommodation up to ₹7,500 per unit per day without ITC |
| 18% | Standard rate for most goods and services, including most professional services |
| 40% | Sin and luxury goods and services: pan masala and tobacco products (from 1 February 2026), aerated sugared beverages, larger motor cars, motorcycles above 350 cc, yachts, and services such as betting and casinos |

The 12% and 28% slabs were largely removed. In the exam, rates are normally given in the question; learn the slabs and the special conditions (5% without ITC for restaurants and budget hotels).

lesson.heading: Worked example and common mistakes
lesson.body:
A composition trader has turnover in the State of ₹80 lakh of taxable goods and ₹15 lakh of exempt goods for the year. Tax is 1% of **taxable** turnover only:

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Taxable turnover | 80,00,000 |
| CGST @ 0.5% | 40,000 |
| SGST @ 0.5% | 40,000 |
| **Composition tax** | **80,000** |

A composition **manufacturer** pays 1% on the entire turnover in the State, including exempt supplies.

**Common mistakes:**
- Paying RCM tax by utilising ITC. RCM tax is always paid in cash.
- Applying RCM on legal services when the recipient is an individual for personal matters. RCM applies only when the recipient is a business entity (and such service is usually exempt anyway).
- Allowing a composition dealer to make inter-State sales. Inter-State outward supply makes him ineligible (inter-State purchases are allowed).
- Charging the 5% composition rate on a restaurant that serves alcohol: such a restaurant is not eligible for composition.

keyPoints: Section 9(1) CGST: max 20%; section 5(1) IGST: max 40%; alcoholic liquor for human consumption excluded.
RCM: section 9(3) notified supplies, 9(4) notified recipients from unregistered persons, 9(5) ECO deemed supplier.
RCM tax must be paid through the electronic cash ledger; ITC of it is then available if not blocked.
Composition 10(1): ₹1.5 crore limit (₹75 lakh special category States); manufacturer 1% of turnover in State, trader 1% of taxable turnover, restaurant 5%.
Composition 10(2A) for services: ₹50 lakh limit, 6%.
Composition: no ITC, no tax collection, bill of supply, CMP-08 quarterly, GSTR-4 annually.
GST 2.0 from 22 September 2025: 5% and 18% main slabs, 40% for sin and luxury items.

cases.title: Case: Annapurna Bhojnalaya
cases.body:
Annapurna Bhojnalaya runs a vegetarian restaurant in Indore, Madhya Pradesh. It does not serve alcohol and is not located in specified premises. It has no other business anywhere in India.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Aggregate turnover, FY 2025-26 | 1,20,00,000 |
| Expected turnover from restaurant service, FY 2026-27 | 1,40,00,000 |
| Expected inward supplies with GST (food items, gas, rent) | 60,00,000 |

The owner is deciding whether to opt for the composition scheme for FY 2026-27. He also plans to start sending packed food to a corporate client in Ujjain (Madhya Pradesh) and to a client in Kota (Rajasthan).

questions.prompt: Which of the following services is taxable under reverse charge under section 9(3)?
options: Legal services by an individual advocate to a registered company
Chartered accountancy services by a CA firm to a company
Legal services by an individual advocate to an individual for a family dispute
Architect services to a builder
questions.explanation: Legal services by an advocate or firm of advocates to a business entity are notified under RCM; the business entity pays. CA and architect services are forward charge. Legal services to an individual not for business are exempt.

questions.prompt: Passenger transport through a ride-hailing app by a driver using his own car is taxed under section 9(5). Who is liable to pay the GST?
options: The driver
The passenger
The electronic commerce operator
No one, as it is exempt
questions.explanation: Section 9(5) and the notification under it deem the ECO to be the supplier of passenger transport by radio taxi, motor cab, maxi cab and motor cycle. The ECO pays the tax as if it were the supplier.

questions.prompt: A trader dealing only in goods made all-India aggregate turnover of ₹1.45 crore in the preceding year and makes some inter-State sales. Is he eligible for the composition scheme under section 10(1)?
options: Yes, as turnover is below ₹1.5 crore
No, because a person making inter-State outward supplies is not eligible
Yes, but only for intra-State sales
No, because the limit for traders is ₹50 lakh
questions.explanation: Section 10(2)(c) excludes persons engaged in inter-State outward supply of goods. The turnover test is met, but the condition fails.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the GST 2.0 rate structure (effective 22 September 2025) is correct?
options: It retained 12% and 28% as the main slabs
It moved to two main slabs of 5% and 18%, with 40% for sin and luxury goods
It introduced a single uniform rate of 15%
It abolished the nil rate
questions.explanation: The 56th GST Council approved 5% and 18% as the main slabs and a special 40% rate for sin and luxury goods. Nil, 0.25% and 3% rates continue for specified goods.

questions.prompt: A registered company may pay GST payable under reverse charge on sponsorship services by utilising its balance in the electronic credit ledger.
questions.explanation: Under section 49(4) read with the Explanation to section 49, the credit ledger can be used only for output tax payable under forward charge. RCM tax must be paid in cash. The company can then claim ITC of that cash payment.

questions.prompt: Which of the following persons are NOT eligible for the composition scheme under section 10(1)? Select all that apply.
options: A manufacturer of ice cream
A trader of footwear with turnover of ₹90 lakh making only intra-State sales
A restaurant serving alcoholic liquor
A casual taxable person
A manufacturer of steel furniture with turnover of ₹1.2 crore making only intra-State sales
questions.explanation: Ice cream manufacturers are a notified excluded class, a restaurant serving alcohol cannot opt, and casual taxable persons are excluded by section 10(2)(e). The footwear trader and furniture manufacturer satisfy the conditions.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: a composition taxpayer issues a ___ of supply instead of a tax invoice.
questions.explanation: Section 31(3)(c): a registered person paying tax under section 10 issues a bill of supply, since it cannot collect tax from the recipient.

questions.prompt: Shakti Ltd, a registered company, receives legal services from an individual advocate in the same State for ₹1,50,000. GST on legal services is 18%. Compute the total GST (CGST + SGST) Shakti Ltd must pay in cash under reverse charge. Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation:
Legal services by an advocate to a business entity are under RCM; the recipient pays.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Value | 1,50,000 |
| CGST @ 9% | 13,500 |
| SGST @ 9% | 13,500 |
| Total RCM payable in cash | 27,000 |

questions.prompt: A composition manufacturer (not of notified goods) has turnover in the State of ₹1,10,00,000 for the year, including ₹10,00,000 of exempt goods. Compute total composition tax (CGST + SGST). Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation:
For manufacturers the rate is 0.5% CGST + 0.5% SGST on the **turnover in the State**, which includes exempt supplies (traders, by contrast, pay only on taxable supplies).

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Turnover in State | 1,10,00,000 |
| CGST @ 0.5% | 55,000 |
| SGST @ 0.5% | 55,000 |
| Total | 1,10,000 |

questions.prompt: A composition trader had turnover in the State of ₹80,00,000 in the preceding financial year. Under section 10(1), what is the maximum value of services (other than restaurant service) it may supply in the current year while staying in the scheme? Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation:
Second proviso to section 10(1): services up to the higher of 10% of turnover in the State in the preceding FY or ₹5 lakh.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| 10% of 80,00,000 | 8,00,000 |
| Fixed limit | 5,00,000 |
| Higher of the two | 8,00,000 |

questions.prompt: Is Annapurna Bhojnalaya eligible to opt for composition for FY 2026-27?
options: Yes, because its aggregate turnover in the preceding FY does not exceed ₹1.5 crore
No, because its expected turnover for FY 2026-27 is above ₹1.2 crore
No, because restaurants can use only the section 10(2A) scheme
Yes, but only if expected turnover is below ₹50 lakh
questions.explanation: Eligibility is tested on aggregate turnover of the preceding FY (₹1.2 crore, within ₹1.5 crore). Restaurant service not serving alcohol is specifically allowed under section 10(1). If turnover in FY 2026-27 crosses ₹1.5 crore, the option lapses from that day.

questions.prompt: If Annapurna opts for composition and achieves the expected turnover, compute its composition tax (CGST + SGST) for FY 2026-27. Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation:
Restaurant service under composition: 2.5% CGST + 2.5% SGST on turnover in the State.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Turnover | 1,40,00,000 |
| CGST @ 2.5% | 3,50,000 |
| SGST @ 2.5% | 3,50,000 |
| Total | 7,00,000 |

Under the regular scheme, restaurant service outside specified premises is also 5% without ITC, but the regular dealer collects the tax from customers; the composition dealer cannot collect it and bears it from his price.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of the planned supply of packed food to the client in Kota if Annapurna is under composition?
options: No effect, as only the Ujjain supply is relevant
It is an inter-State outward supply of goods, which makes Annapurna ineligible to continue in composition
It is allowed because restaurants may make inter-State supplies up to ₹5 lakh
It must be billed under reverse charge
questions.explanation: A composition taxpayer cannot make inter-State outward supplies of goods (section 10(2)(c)). Supplying to Rajasthan would end eligibility. Supplies within Madhya Pradesh (Ujjain) are fine.

questions.prompt: Rajdhani Ltd, registered in Delhi, provides the following details for October 2026 (all values exclusive of GST). Compute its total GST liability, showing forward charge and reverse charge separately. Ignore ITC.
questions.data:
| No. | Particulars | ₹ | Rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Intra-State sales of goods | 10,00,000 | 18% |
| 2 | Inter-State sales of goods | 6,00,000 | 5% |
| 3 | Sponsorship of an event by a sports club in Delhi | 2,00,000 | 18% |
| 4 | Legal fees to an advocate located in Mumbai | 1,00,000 | 18% |
| 5 | Sitting fees to an independent director residing in Delhi | 50,000 | 18% |
| 6 | Salary to a whole-time director (taxed as salary) | 3,00,000 | - |
questions.answer:
| No. | Treatment | CGST (₹) | SGST (₹) | IGST (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Forward charge, intra-State | 90,000 | 90,000 | - |
| 2 | Forward charge, inter-State | - | - | 30,000 |
| | **Forward charge total** | **90,000** | **90,000** | **30,000** |
| 3 | RCM: sponsorship to body corporate; Delhi to Delhi | 18,000 | 18,000 | - |
| 4 | RCM: legal services to business entity; place of supply is Delhi (registered recipient), supplier in Maharashtra, so inter-State | - | - | 18,000 |
| 5 | RCM: services by director (not as employee) | 4,500 | 4,500 | - |

Forward charge liability = ₹2,10,000. Reverse charge liability = ₹63,000, payable only through the electronic cash ledger. **Total = ₹2,73,000.**

questions.prompt: State the conditions and restrictions that apply to a registered person opting for the composition levy under section 10(1).
questions.answer:
- Aggregate turnover in the preceding FY up to ₹1.5 crore (₹75 lakh in specified special category States).
- Not a supplier of services other than restaurant service, except services up to the higher of 10% of turnover in the State or ₹5 lakh.
- No supply of goods not leviable to tax, no inter-State outward supply of goods, no supply through an ECO required to collect TCS, not a manufacturer of notified goods (such as ice cream, pan masala, tobacco).
- Not a casual taxable person or non-resident taxable person.
- All registrations under the same PAN must opt for the scheme.
- Cannot collect tax from recipients and cannot claim ITC; issues bill of supply with the prescribed declaration.
- Must mention 'composition taxable person' on signboards; pays RCM tax at normal rates.
- Pays tax quarterly in CMP-08 and files GSTR-4 annually; option lapses from the day turnover exceeds the limit.

chapters.title: Place of Supply: Intra-State vs Inter-State
chapters.summary: How location of supplier and place of supply decide whether CGST + SGST or IGST is charged, with the basic place of supply rules for goods and services within India.
chapters.lawAsOf: IGST Act 2017 (sections 7, 8, 10 and 12) as amended by the Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Why place of supply matters
lesson.body:
GST is a destination-based tax. The **place of supply** (POS) decides which State gets the tax and, read with the **location of the supplier**, whether the supply is intra-State or inter-State.

| Location of supplier vs place of supply | Nature | Tax |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Same State or same UT | Intra-State (section 8 IGST Act) | CGST + SGST/UTGST |
| Different States, or State and UT, or two UTs | Inter-State (section 7 IGST Act) | IGST |

Deemed **inter-State** supplies irrespective of location (section 7):
- Import of goods, until they cross the customs frontier, and import of services.
- Supplies when the supplier is in India and the place of supply is outside India (exports).
- Supplies to or by a **Special Economic Zone** developer or unit, even within the same State.
- Supplies to a foreign tourist who carries the goods out of India (section 15 refund).
- Any supply in the taxable territory not otherwise intra-State.

Charging CGST + SGST where IGST was due (or vice versa) does not count as payment: the correct tax must be paid and a refund of the wrong tax claimed (section 77 CGST / section 19 IGST), without interest.

lesson.heading: Place of supply of goods within India: section 10
lesson.body:
| Situation | Place of supply |
| --- | --- |
| Supply involves movement of goods (by supplier, recipient or any other person) | Location where movement terminates for delivery to the recipient - 10(1)(a) |
| Goods delivered to a recipient or any other person on the direction of a third person (bill-to-ship-to) | Principal place of business of the third person - 10(1)(b) |
| No movement of goods | Location of goods at the time of delivery to the recipient - 10(1)(c) |
| Goods assembled or installed at site | Place of assembly or installation - 10(1)(d) |
| Goods supplied on board a conveyance (train, aircraft, vessel, motor vehicle) | Location where the goods are taken on board - 10(1)(e) |

**Bill-to-ship-to example:** A of Delhi orders goods from B of Haryana and asks B to deliver them to C, A's customer in Delhi. Two supplies arise:

| Supply | Location of supplier | Place of supply | Tax |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B to A | Haryana | Delhi (A's principal place of business, deemed received by A) | IGST |
| A to C | Delhi | Delhi (movement terminates at C) | CGST + SGST |

lesson.heading: Place of supply of services within India: section 12 (basic rules)
lesson.body:
**General rule, section 12(2):** if the recipient is **registered**, POS is the location of the recipient. If unregistered, POS is the recipient's address on record, failing which the location of the supplier.

Key specific rules (override the general rule):

| Service | Place of supply |
| --- | --- |
| Services related to immovable property, including hotel accommodation - 12(3) | Location of the immovable property |
| Restaurant, catering, personal grooming, fitness, beauty and health services - 12(4) | Where the services are actually performed |
| Training and performance appraisal - 12(5) | Registered recipient: his location; otherwise where performed |
| Admission to an event or amusement park - 12(6) | Where the event is held or park is located |
| Transportation of goods including courier - 12(8) | Registered recipient: his location; otherwise where goods are handed over for transport |
| Passenger transportation - 12(9) | Registered recipient: his location; otherwise where the passenger embarks for a continuous journey |
| Banking and financial services - 12(12) | Location of recipient on supplier's records; otherwise location of supplier |

The Inter syllabus focuses on applying these rules to decide intra-State vs inter-State. Cross-border rules (section 13) are for the Final level.

lesson.heading: Worked example and common mistakes
lesson.body:
A Goa hotel lets 2 rooms for 3 nights at ₹6,000 per room per night to a company registered in Mumbai. Under section 12(3) the POS is the location of the hotel (Goa). Supplier and POS are both in Goa, so the supply is intra-State even though the guest is from Maharashtra.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Value 2 x 3 x 6,000 | 36,000 |
| CGST @ 2.5% (tariff up to ₹7,500 per day) | 900 |
| SGST @ 2.5% | 900 |

The Mumbai company cannot take credit of Goa's SGST in its Maharashtra registration.

**Common mistakes:**
- Using the recipient's billing address for goods that move: POS is where movement terminates.
- Forgetting that supplies to an SEZ unit in the same State are inter-State.
- Applying the general rule to hotel stays or restaurant meals; specific rules prevail.
- Treating over-the-counter sales to an out-of-State customer as inter-State: delivery happens at the shop, so the supply is intra-State.

keyPoints: Supplier location and place of supply in the same State/UT: intra-State, CGST + SGST/UTGST. Otherwise: inter-State, IGST.
Supplies to or by SEZ units/developers, imports and exports are always inter-State.
Goods with movement: where movement terminates (10(1)(a)); bill-to-ship-to: principal place of business of the third person (10(1)(b)).
No movement: location of goods at delivery; installation at site: place of installation; on board a conveyance: where taken on board.
Services general rule 12(2): registered recipient's location; unregistered: address on record, else supplier's location.
Immovable property and hotels: location of property; restaurant and beauty services: where performed; events: where held.
Wrong tax paid (IGST vs CGST + SGST): pay correct tax, claim refund of the wrong tax, no interest.

cases.title: Case: Deccan Tech Supplies
cases.body:
Deccan Tech Supplies is registered only in Bengaluru, Karnataka. Its supplies in December 2026 (values exclusive of GST; all taxable at 18%):

| No. | Supply | Value (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Laptops sold to a registered dealer in Chennai; Deccan ships them from Bengaluru to Chennai | 4,00,000 |
| 2 | Printers sold to Kapoor & Co, Delhi, who directs Deccan to deliver them to Kapoor's customer in Mysuru, Karnataka | 3,00,000 |
| 3 | A printer sold over the counter in the Bengaluru store to a visitor from Kochi, Kerala, who carries it home | 50,000 |
| 4 | A server rack supplied and installed at a client's data centre in Hyderabad, Telangana | 6,00,000 |
| 5 | Annual maintenance services to a registered client in Pune, Maharashtra | 1,00,000 |
| 6 | A one-day training session for an unregistered individual, held at Deccan's Bengaluru office | 20,000 |

questions.prompt: A supplier in Ahmedabad sells goods to an SEZ unit located in Gandhinagar, Gujarat. The supply is:
options: Intra-State, CGST + SGST
Inter-State, IGST
Outside GST
Intra-State, UTGST
questions.explanation: Section 7(5)(b) IGST Act: supply of goods or services to an SEZ developer or unit is inter-State, even when supplier and SEZ are in the same State. Such supplies are zero-rated.

questions.prompt: What is the place of supply of goods supplied on board an aircraft flying from Mumbai to Kolkata, where the goods were taken on board at Mumbai?
options: Kolkata
Mumbai
Location of the airline's head office
Location of the passenger's home
questions.explanation: Section 10(1)(e): for goods supplied on board a conveyance, the place of supply is the location at which the goods are taken on board.

questions.prompt: A beauty salon in Lucknow provides services to a customer registered in Bihar who walks in for a session. The place of supply is:
options: Bihar, being the location of the registered recipient
Uttar Pradesh, where the service is performed
Location of the salon's head office
Either State at the supplier's option
questions.explanation: Section 12(4): personal grooming, beauty treatment, fitness and health services have their place of supply where the services are actually performed. The registration status of the recipient does not matter.

questions.prompt: If a supplier charges CGST and SGST on a supply that is actually inter-State, the tax paid can be adjusted against IGST payable without any further payment.
questions.explanation: Under section 77 CGST Act and section 19 IGST Act, the supplier must pay the correct tax (IGST) and claim a refund of the CGST and SGST wrongly paid. No interest is payable on the correct tax in such cases, but adjustment is not allowed.

questions.prompt: Which of these are inter-State supplies? Select all that apply.
options: Supply by a Pune supplier to a recipient in Pune, where goods are delivered in Pune
Supply of goods by a Pune supplier to an SEZ unit in Pune
Import of goods into Mumbai until they cross the customs frontier
Hotel accommodation in Shimla provided by a Shimla hotel to a guest registered in Delhi
Goods moved by a Surat supplier to a buyer's warehouse in Jaipur
questions.explanation: SEZ supplies and imports are inter-State by section 7. Surat to Jaipur involves goods moving across States. The Pune-to-Pune sale is intra-State, and the hotel stay has POS at the hotel's location (Himachal Pradesh), the same as the supplier's location, so it is intra-State.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: where a supply of goods does not involve movement of goods, the place of supply is the location of such goods at the time of ___ to the recipient.
questions.explanation: Section 10(1)(c) IGST Act. For example, a building owner selling a generator installed in the building, where the generator is not moved.

questions.prompt: A hotel in Goa lets 2 rooms for 3 nights at ₹6,000 per room per night (exclusive of GST) to a company registered in Mumbai. GST on accommodation with value up to ₹7,500 per unit per day is 5%. Compute the SGST charged by the hotel. Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation:
Section 12(3): POS for accommodation is the location of the hotel (Goa). Supplier is also in Goa, so CGST + SGST apply.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Value 2 x 3 x 6,000 | 36,000 |
| CGST @ 2.5% | 900 |
| SGST @ 2.5% | 900 |

questions.prompt: A of Delhi orders goods from B of Gurugram (Haryana) for ₹4,00,000 and asks B to deliver them directly to C, A's customer in Delhi. A charges C ₹4,60,000. All values are exclusive of GST; rate 18%. Compute the total GST (CGST + SGST + IGST) charged by A on its supply to C. Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation:
Supply B to A: POS is A's principal place of business (Delhi) under section 10(1)(b); supplier in Haryana, so IGST 72,000.

Supply A to C: goods move to C in Delhi, supplier in Delhi, so intra-State.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Value | 4,60,000 |
| CGST @ 9% | 41,400 |
| SGST @ 9% | 41,400 |
| Total | 82,800 |

questions.prompt: What tax does Deccan charge on supply 2 (printers delivered to Mysuru on the direction of Kapoor & Co, Delhi)?
options: CGST + SGST of Karnataka, since goods move within Karnataka
IGST, since the place of supply is Kapoor's principal place of business in Delhi
No tax, as Kapoor will pay
CGST + SGST of Delhi
questions.explanation: Section 10(1)(b): goods delivered on the direction of a third person are deemed received by that third person, and POS is his principal place of business (Delhi). Supplier in Karnataka, POS Delhi: IGST.

questions.prompt: What is the nature of supply 3 (over-the-counter sale to the visitor from Kerala)?
options: Inter-State, because the buyer lives in Kerala
Intra-State, because delivery takes place in Bengaluru
Export of goods
Not a supply
questions.explanation: The supplier delivers the goods at its store in Bengaluru. POS is where the goods are delivered to the recipient (Karnataka), the same as the supplier's location, so CGST + SGST apply.

questions.prompt: Compute the total IGST payable by Deccan Tech Supplies for December 2026. Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation:
| No. | Place of supply | Nature | IGST @ 18% (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Chennai, where movement ends - 10(1)(a) | Inter-State | 72,000 |
| 2 | Delhi, third person's principal place - 10(1)(b) | Inter-State | 54,000 |
| 3 | Bengaluru, delivery at store | Intra-State | - |
| 4 | Hyderabad, place of installation - 10(1)(d) | Inter-State | 1,08,000 |
| 5 | Pune, registered recipient - 12(2) | Inter-State | 18,000 |

questions.prompt: Explain the place of supply of goods in a bill-to-ship-to transaction under section 10(1)(b) of the IGST Act, with an example of the two supplies involved.
questions.answer:
- Where goods are delivered by the supplier to a recipient or any other person on the direction of a third person (as agent or otherwise), before or during movement, the third person is deemed to have received the goods.
- POS of that supply is the principal place of business of the third person.
- Example: A (Delhi) buys from B (Haryana) and asks B to ship to C in Delhi.
- Supply 1, B to A: supplier in Haryana, POS Delhi (A's principal place of business): IGST charged by B to A.
- Supply 2, A to C: supplier in Delhi, goods delivered in Delhi: CGST + SGST charged by A to C.
- The rule lets A take ITC of B's IGST in its own State and ensures the tax follows the ordering party, even though the goods never reach A.

chapters.title: Exemptions from GST
chapters.summary: The power to exempt under section 11, absolute vs conditional exemptions, and the main exempt goods and services tested at Inter: health care, education, agriculture, charity, legal services, renting and insurance.
chapters.lawAsOf: CGST Act section 11 and exemption notifications for goods and services as amended up to the GST 2.0 changes effective 22 September 2025, read with the Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Power to grant exemption: section 11
lesson.body:
Section 11(1): the Government may, on the GST Council's recommendation, exempt goods or services generally, **absolutely or subject to conditions**, by notification, in public interest. Section 11(2): it may also exempt by **special order** in exceptional circumstances, for a specific case, stating the reasons.

| Point | Absolute exemption | Conditional exemption |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Conditions | None | Must satisfy stated conditions |
| Can supplier pay tax instead? | No. Where exemption is absolute, the registered person shall not collect tax on such supply | Supplier may choose not to avail it |

An **exempt supply** (section 2(47)) includes supplies taxable at nil rate, wholly exempt under section 11 (or section 6 IGST), and non-taxable supplies. Exempt supplies are counted in aggregate turnover, and ITC attributable to them must be reversed (section 17(2)).

lesson.heading: Key exempt services
lesson.body:
| Category | Exempt services (summary of the services exemption notification) |
| --- | --- |
| Charity | Charitable activities by an entity registered under section 12AB of the Income-tax Act, such as public health, advancement of religion, spirituality or yoga, and education programmes for abandoned or orphaned children |
| Health care | Health care services by a clinical establishment, authorised medical practitioner or para-medics. Not exempt: hair transplant and cosmetic or plastic surgery, unless done to restore anatomy or functions affected by congenital defect, developmental abnormality, injury or trauma |
| Education | Services by an educational institution to its students, faculty and staff. Services to a school up to higher secondary: transport of students and staff, catering including mid-day meals, security, cleaning and housekeeping in the school, and services relating to admission or conduct of examination |
| Legal | Services by an advocate or firm of advocates (other than representational services before a court by a senior advocate) to an advocate or firm of advocates, to any person other than a business entity, or to a business entity with aggregate turnover in the preceding FY up to the registration threshold (₹20 lakh / ₹10 lakh) |
| Renting | Renting of residential dwelling for use as residence, except where let to a registered person (a registered proprietor renting for personal residence, not on business account, remains exempt) |
| Agriculture | Cultivation, supply of farm labour, harvesting, warehousing of agricultural produce, renting of agro machinery, services of APMCs |
| Insurance | Individual life insurance and individual health insurance policies (including reinsurance), exempt from 22 September 2025 |
| Government and RBI | Services by the Reserve Bank of India; pure services to Government in relation to Panchayat or Municipality functions |
| Others | Transfer of a going concern; admission to museums, national parks, zoos and protected monuments; services by way of training or coaching in recreational activities relating to arts, culture or sports by an individual |

lesson.heading: Key exempt goods
lesson.body:
The nil-rate notification for goods covers essentials, typically when not pre-packaged and labelled:
- Fresh fruits and vegetables, fresh milk, curd and lassi, eggs, unprocessed cereals and pulses (not pre-packaged and labelled).
- Natural honey, unpacked salt, jaggery, puffed rice.
- Books, newspapers, maps; judicial and non-judicial stamp papers.
- Human blood and its components; contraceptives.

The GST 2.0 notifications (22 September 2025) moved further items to nil, including ultra-high temperature (UHT) milk, pre-packaged paneer, Indian breads such as roti and paratha, and specified life-saving drugs. Check the current notification for exact entries before relying on any single item.

lesson.heading: Worked example and common mistakes
lesson.body:
Dr Mehra, a registered surgeon in Pune, receives during the year:

| Receipt | ₹ | Treatment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Consultation and surgery (illness) | 12,00,000 | Exempt health care |
| Hair transplant for cosmetic reasons | 3,00,000 | Taxable |
| Rent from a shop let to a chemist | 6,00,000 | Taxable |
| Rent from a flat let to a family for residence | 2,40,000 | Exempt |
| **Taxable value** | **9,00,000** | GST @ 18% = **1,62,000** |

**Common mistakes:**
- Exempting all services by a hospital: cosmetic procedures are taxable.
- Treating residential rent as exempt where the tenant is a registered person. The registered tenant pays GST under RCM.
- Exempting construction services to a private school: only the listed services to schools are exempt.
- Treating every service by a charitable trust as exempt: only charitable activities are; renting a hall for weddings is taxable.

keyPoints: Section 11(1): exemption by notification, absolute or conditional, on Council recommendation; 11(2): special order in exceptional cases.
No tax may be collected on absolutely exempt supplies.
Exempt supply (section 2(47)) includes nil-rated, wholly exempt and non-taxable supplies.
Health care exempt, except cosmetic or plastic surgery and hair transplant (unless reconstructive).
Services to schools up to higher secondary: transport, catering, security, cleaning, admission and exam services are exempt.
Advocate services exempt to non-business persons and business entities with turnover up to ₹20 lakh (₹10 lakh special category); otherwise RCM.
Individual life and health insurance exempt from 22 September 2025.

chapters.title: Time and Value of Supply
chapters.summary: When the liability to pay GST arises (sections 12 and 13) and on what amount (section 15 and the valuation rules), including inclusions, discounts and pure agent expenses.
chapters.lawAsOf: CGST Act sections 12, 13 and 15 and CGST Rules 27 to 35, as amended by the Finance Act 2026

lesson.heading: Time of supply of goods: section 12
lesson.body:
**Forward charge, section 12(2):** time of supply is the earlier of:
- date of issue of invoice, or the last date by which the invoice should have been issued under section 31; and
- date of receipt of payment (earlier of entry in books and credit in bank).

By Notification 66/2017-CT, GST on **advances received for goods** is not payable by any registered person other than a composition taxpayer. So in practice the time of supply of goods is the invoice date (or due date of invoice). If the supplier receives up to ₹1,000 in excess of the invoice amount, he may treat the invoice date as the time of supply for the excess.

**Reverse charge, section 12(3):** earliest of (a) date of receipt of goods, (b) date of payment (earlier of entry in recipient's books and debit in bank), (c) date immediately after 30 days from the date of the supplier's invoice. If none can be determined, date of entry in the recipient's books.

**Vouchers, section 12(4):** date of issue if the supply is identifiable at that point; otherwise date of redemption.

lesson.heading: Time of supply of services: section 13
lesson.body:
Invoice for services must be issued within **30 days** of supply (45 days for banks, insurers and NBFCs) under rule 47.

| Situation, section 13(2) | Time of supply |
| --- | --- |
| Invoice issued within the prescribed period | Earlier of invoice date and date of payment |
| Invoice not issued within the prescribed period | Earlier of date of provision of service and date of payment |
| Neither (a) nor (b) applies | Date the recipient shows receipt in his books |

Advances for services **are** taxable: the date of advance is the time of supply for that amount. Excess up to ₹1,000 over invoice value may be taxed at invoice date at the supplier's option.

**Reverse charge, section 13(3):** earlier of (a) date of payment and (b) date immediately after **60 days** from the supplier's invoice. For associated enterprises where the supplier is outside India: earlier of entry in the recipient's books and date of payment.

Section 14 decides the time of supply when the rate changes between supply, invoice and payment.

lesson.heading: Value of supply: section 15
lesson.body:
Value is the **transaction value**: the price actually paid or payable, where supplier and recipient are not related and price is the sole consideration (section 15(1)).

| Included in value - section 15(2) | Excluded from value |
| --- | --- |
| Taxes, duties, cesses, fees and charges under any law other than GST, if charged separately by the supplier | CGST, SGST, UTGST, IGST and GST compensation cess |
| Any amount the supplier is liable to pay but which the recipient pays, not included in price | Discount given before or at the time of supply, recorded in the invoice - 15(3)(a) |
| Incidental expenses such as commission and packing charged by the supplier, and anything done by the supplier at the time of or before delivery | Post-supply discount where the conditions of 15(3)(b) are met |
| Interest, late fee or penalty for delayed payment of consideration | Subsidies provided by the Central and State Governments |
| Subsidies directly linked to price, from non-Government sources | Expenses incurred as a pure agent of the recipient (rule 33) |

**Post-supply discount, section 15(3)(b):** traditionally excluded only if established by an agreement entered into before or at the time of supply, specifically linked to the relevant invoices, and the recipient reverses ITC attributable to the discount. The Finance Act 2026 substitutes clause (b) to remove the pre-agreement and invoice-linking requirement, so a discount given through a credit note under section 34 is excluded if the recipient reverses the attributable ITC. Check the commencement notification and ICAI's applicability notice for your attempt.

**Valuation rules** apply where transaction value cannot be used, such as supplies between related or distinct persons (rule 28: open market value; where the recipient is eligible for full ITC, the invoice value is deemed open market value), supplies through an agent (rule 29) and residual cases (rules 30, 31).

lesson.heading: Pure agent and common mistakes
lesson.body:
**Rule 33 - pure agent:** expenditure incurred as a pure agent of the recipient is excluded from value if all conditions hold: (i) the supplier acts as a pure agent of the recipient when making payment to a third party on the recipient's authorisation; (ii) the payment is separately indicated in the invoice; (iii) the supplies procured are in addition to the services the supplier supplies on his own account.

A pure agent: has a contractual agreement with the recipient to act as his agent in incurring expenses; neither intends to hold nor holds title to the goods or services; does not use them for his own interest; and receives only the actual amount incurred.

**Common mistakes:**
- Charging GST on advances for goods. Not payable after Notification 66/2017-CT.
- Excluding a State Government subsidy from value but including a Central one, or vice versa: both Government subsidies are excluded.
- Including GST itself in the value of supply.
- Treating late payment interest as outside the value: it is included under section 15(2)(d).
- Excluding packing charged separately: incidental expenses charged by the supplier are included.

keyPoints: Goods (forward charge): earlier of invoice (or due date) and payment; no GST on advances for goods (Notification 66/2017-CT).
Goods (RCM): earliest of receipt of goods, payment, and day after 30 days from invoice.
Services: invoice within 30 days (45 for banks/insurers/NBFCs); if issued in time, earlier of invoice and payment, else earlier of provision and payment.
Services (RCM): earlier of payment and day after 60 days from invoice.
Section 15(2) inclusions: other taxes, supplier's liabilities paid by recipient, incidental expenses, late payment interest, non-Government subsidies linked to price.
Exclusions: GST itself, discounts in invoice, qualifying post-supply discounts, Government subsidies, pure agent expenses (rule 33).
Finance Act 2026 substitutes section 15(3)(b): post-supply discount via credit note with ITC reversal by recipient; verify commencement for your attempt.

questions.prompt: Explain the conditions under which a supplier is treated as a pure agent and when expenses incurred as a pure agent are excluded from the value of supply.
questions.answer:
- Rule 33 CGST Rules excludes expenditure incurred as a pure agent of the recipient from the value of supply.
- A pure agent (Explanation to rule 33): enters into a contractual agreement with the recipient to act as his pure agent to incur expenditure in the course of supply; neither intends to hold nor holds any title to the goods or services so procured; does not use them for his own interest; receives only the actual amount incurred.
- Conditions for exclusion: (i) the supplier acts as pure agent when making payment to the third party on authorisation by the recipient; (ii) the payment is separately indicated in the invoice; (iii) the supplies procured from the third party are in addition to the services supplied on his own account.
- Example: a CA paying ROC filing fees for a client and recovering the exact amount, shown separately in the invoice.

chapters.summary: Eligibility and conditions for ITC under section 16, apportionment under section 17(1)-(2) and rule 42, the blocked credits of section 17(5), and the 180-day payment and time-limit rules.
